(i) the alpA and ssrA genes are part of a P4 prophage, (ii) the Alp proteolytic activity is regulated at the level of RNA processing, and (iii) the Alp and Lon proteases are functionally related.

the cryptic prophages in E. coli K-12 are excised by a SlpA integrase, that excision is necessary for expression of the Alpl protease, and that excision is sufficient to inactivate 10Sa RNA, a negative regulator of Alpl expression.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the control of the Alp (and Lon) proteolytic systems.
the regulation of the Alp and Lon proteases
the expression of a new protease in E. coli, and we have found that the expression of this protease is dependent on a P4-like prophase.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
AlpA is a positive transcriptional activator of slpA and of the ssrA RNA.

a cryptic prophage in E. coli K-12, when excised by a mechanism involving a SlpA integrase and the integration host factor, leads to increased expression of a previously uncharacterized energy-dependent protease, the Alp, which is necessary for suppression of the lon mutation.

the alpA and ssrA genes act as regulators of the Alp proteinase, that slpA acts as a regulator of alpA, that the alp and slp genes are located within a P4-like prophagic element, that the prophage can be excised by a process dependent on the SlpA integrase, and that excision is necessary for full expression of Alp protease activity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a cryptic prophage is a negative regulator of Alp protease synthesis, and excision of this prophage leads to protease expression.
the cryptic prophase is a regulator of the Alp and Slp proteins, which are regulators of protease expression.
the cryptic prophages in E. coli are not only a source of genes for new functions but are also important in regulating expression of genes for existing functions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a prophage can be used as a tool to regulate gene expression in E. coli.
a cryptic P-like prophage, present in all E. coli strains, can be excised and lost, and that excision and loss are necessary for expression of the suppressing protease, the Alp protein.
a prophage can be a source of new regulatory genes that affect host physiology.
